english_translation: It has rained today, so we should delay going to the field.

dialogue.shona: Mvura yanaya nhasi, saka tinofanira kunonoka kuenda kumunda.
dialogue.english: It has rained today, so we should delay going to the field.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mvura [water / rain] • yanaya [yanaya] • nhasi [today] • saka [so / therefore] • tinofanira [we fanira] • kunonoka [to / at nonoka] • kuenda [to / at enda] • kumunda [to / at munda]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yanaya')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yanaya' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('tinofanira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'tinofanira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kunonoka')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kunonoka' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Working with Heavy Clay Soils ('Ivhu Rinomira Mvura') After Rain
cultural_notes.content: When heavy rain falls at dawn ('mvura yanaya nhasi'), farmers wait a little before entering the field ('kunonoka kuenda kumunda') so the wet topsoil drains slightly and does not cling heavily to hoes and boots.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.

active_exercises.prompt: If a farmer says 'Gore rino takawana goho guru pamunda pedu', what happened?
options: They are waiting for the rain to start next month
The river flooded and washed away the bridge
A strong wind blew from the east all afternoon
They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
active_exercises.correct_answer: They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
active_exercises.explanation: 'Takawana' = 'we obtained/got', 'goho guru' = 'a big harvest', 'pamunda pedu' = 'from our field'.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this new sentence in the past tense: 'Nezuro amai ______ sadza nenyama.' (Yesterday Mother cooked sadza and meat.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Amai' takes the respectful plural past prefix 'vaka-' + '-bika' (cook) -> 'vakabika' ('cooked').
